the learned Single Judge, while holding the contempt petition not maintainable, has imposed costs of Rs.25000/- upon the appellant herein for filing a false and frivolous contempt petition and suppressing the material facts.

2 At the outset, Mr. J.H.Reshi learned counsel for the appellant would submit that the appellant is not pressing this appeal as against the impugned order to the extent of dismissing the contempt petition as not maintainable.
He would fairly submit that the order passed by the learned Single Judge dismissing the contempt petition is not appealable under clause 12 of the Letters Patent.

Mr.
Reshi learned counsel would, therefore, confine this appeal only insofaras and to the extent the learned Single Judge has imposed costs of Rs.25000/- on the appellant by terming the contempt petition filed by him as 'false and frivolous'.

3 Indisputably, under Article 215 of the Constitution of India and the provisions of the Contempt of Courts Act, a Court hearing a contempt plea is not competent to impose costs on the person invoking the contempt jurisdiction on the ground that the contempt petition is based on false and flimsy grounds or that there is suppression and concealment of material facts.
The imposition of costs in such situation could only be traced to the inherent power of the Court to act ex debito justitiae.

Viewed thus, we are in agreement with the learned counsel for the appellant that the order insofar as and to the extent it imposes costs upon the appellant is appealable under clause 12 of the Letters Patent.
4 Learned counsel appearing for the respondentsMr. Mohsin Qadri learned Sr AAG also did not raise objection to the maintainability of the appeal to the aforesaid extent.

He, however,
would submit that the appellant invoked the contempt jurisdiction of this Court on totally false and flimsy grounds and, therefore, wasted precious time of the Court.

The learned Single Judge was,
therefore, correct in reprimanding the appellant and imposing exemplary costs of Rs.25000/- upon him.

5 Before we proceed to appreciate the rival contentions of the parties to arrive at just conclusion, we deem it appropriate to trace briefly the factual antecedents leading to filing of this appeal by the appellant.

6 Land measuring 10 kanals for construction of Fire and Emergency Services, District Complex,
Anantnag was identified at Sarnal, Anantnag and, accordingly, on the indent issued by the Department of Fire and Emergency Services, Acquisition proceedings were initiated by the Collector Land Acquisition, Anantnag (ACR) ['the Collector'] under Jammu and KashmirLand Acquisition Act, 1934 ['the Act'].

sentences.text: On conclusion of the acquisition proceedings, a final award to the tune of Rs.17,25,000/- was passed by the Collector in the year 1999.
The Department of Fire and Emergency Services deposited the entire award amount with the Collector in the year 1999 itself and took over the possession of the acquired land.

7 The land owners were not satisfied with the rate per kanal fixed by the Collector and, therefore,
made an application under Section 18 of the Act for making reference to the Court of Principal District Judge, Anantnag ['PDJ'].

sentences.text: This application was allowed by the Deputy Commissioner Anantnag as District Collector Land Acquisition on 06.07.2006 and, accordingly, reference was made to the Court of PDJ, Anantnag under Section 18 of the Act.

While the reference proceedings Gull Mohammad Bhat Aged 66 Years Son Of ... vs Mr Raj Kumar Goyal Financial ... on 12 July, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/57326716/
2 were pending before the Court of PDJ, Anantnag, the land owners including the appellant herein moved an application under Section 35 of the Act seeking a direction to the Department of Fire and Emergency Services to deposit the amount payable on the award by way of statutory interest.

sentences.text: The Department of Fire and Emergency Services was also impleaded as party respondent in the reference.
The application was objected to by the respondents.

However, the Court of PDJ,
Anantnag vide its order dated 27.03.2010 directed the Collector to deposit the awarded amount along with interest at the rate of 6%per annum for the first year from the date of taking over the possession of the land and with further interest at the rate of 10% per annum forthe subsequent years with the Nazir of the Court.

8 Feeling aggrieved by the order of Reference Court (PDJ, Anantnag), the respondents filed OWP No. 243/2016 before a Single Judge of this Court,primarily,on the ground that the Department of Fire and Emergency Services had deposited the awarded amount well within time with the Collector and it is only because of failure of the Collector to disburse the amount in time to the interested persons, the Department of Fire and Emergency Services is being burdened with the liability of statutory interest.

sentences.text: The writ petition was entertained by the learned Single Judge and vide order dated 06.02.2016, the operation of order passed by the Reference Court was stayed.
However, OWP No. 243/2016 was ultimately dismissed by the learned Single Judge vide its order dated 18.01.2019.
LPA No. 157/2019 filed by the respondents to challenge the order passed by the learned Single Judge was also dismissed by a Division Bench of this Court vide order dated 19.02.2021.
The respondents even approached the Supreme Court by way of SLP No. 13206/2021 which was dismissed as withdrawn vide order dated 18.11.2021.

9 With the dismissal of SLP, the execution proceedings which were pending adjudication before the Reference Court came to be revived with respect to payment of statutory interest in terms of Section 35 of the Act.

While the execution proceedings were pending in respect of the order passed with reference to Section 35 of the Act, the Reference Court disposed of the Reference finally vide order dated 15.09.2018 and held the land owners including the appellant herein entitled to compensation of Rs.74,75,000/- with interest payable at therate of 6% per annum from 07.07.1999 i.ethe date of taking over of possession of the land till the awarded amount is deposited in the Court.

Notwithstanding the disposal of reference proceedings, the Court of PDJ, Anantnag proceeded with the execution proceedings qua its order dated 27.03.2010 passed in an application filed by the appellants and others under Section 35 of the Act and passed an order on 26.3.2022 and directed the respondents-Department of Fire and Emergency Services to deposit the accrued statutory interest in the Court by or before the next date of hearing, failing which, respondent No.2 in the application would remain present in person in the Court.

The Department of Fire and Emergency Services appeared before the Court of PDJ Anantnag and took objection with regard to maintainability of the execution proceedings in the wake of passing of the final award in the reference proceedings.

sentences.text: When the objection raised by the respondents-Department of Fire and Emergency Services was not entertained by the Executing Court (Court of PDJ, Anantnag), the respondents-Department filed CM(M) No. 178/2022 invoking the supervisory jurisdiction vested in this Court under Article 227 of the Constitution of India.

3 and others' in this Court.

In the application for interim relief, a Single Judge of this Court had, while issuing notice to the other side, directed theappellants- Department to deposit 50% of the awarded amount before the Registry of this Court and stayed the operation of the award and decree dated 15.09.2018 passed by the Reference Court.

In CM(M) No.178/2022, a Single Judge of this Court,
while issuing notice to the other side for filing objections, stayed the operation of the order passed by the Executing Court on 03.09.2022.
10

The appellant, who was a party respondent in the petition, instead of causing appearance in the matter and contesting the petition on merit, filed a contempt petition against the respondents herein for having filed a petition under Article 227 of the Constitution of India despite being aware that the order passed by the Executing Court on 27.03.2010 directing the respondents to deposit the statutory interest in the Court stood upheld up to the level of Supreme Court.

The appellant alleged that the decision of the respondents to challenge the order of Executing Court dated 26.03.2022,
which was nothing, but reiteration of order dated 27.03.2010, was aimed at overreaching the process of law.

It was argued before the learned Single Judge that the respondentswith a view to avoid compliance of order dated 27.03.2010 which had since attained finality and also to overreach the process of law, filed a false and frivolous petition under Article 227 of the Constitution and succeeded in persuading the Court to stay the operation of order of Executing Court which was passed in continuation of order dated 27.03.2010.
It was, thus, argued that the conduct exhibited by the respondents was contemptuous and, therefore, they were liable to be proceeded for committing contempt of the Court.

The contempt petition was contested by the respondents and the plea taken by the respondents before the Single Judge was that by filing a petition under Article 227 of the Constitution of India, therespondents were only exercising their legitimate right of seeking judicial review of the order passed by the Executing Court and, therefore, their action cannot be termed as 'malafide' much less contemptuous in nature.
11

The entire matter was considered by the learned Single Judge at length and it was concluded by the learned Single Judge that the appellant (the petitioner before him) was not entitled in law to seek dismissal of the petition filed under Article 227 of the Constitution by resorting to arm-twisting and filing a contempt petition against the respondents.

The learned Single Judge also came to the conclusion that on facts no contempt was made out, for, there was neither any violation of the orders passed by this Court, nor the respondents by exercising their legitimate right of seeking judicial review of the orders passed by the Executing Court could be said to have committed any contempt.

The learned Single Judge found the entire exercise undertaken by the appellant invoking Article 227 of the Constitution of India read with Section 2 of Contempt of Courts Act based on false and flimsy grounds and, accordingly, dismissed the contempt petition with exemplary costs of Rs.25,000/- vide order and judgment impugned in this appeal.

12 Having heard learned counsel for the parties and perused the material on record, we are of the considered opinion that exercising legitimate right of seeking judicial review before this Court of the orders passed by the Courts subordinate to it by taking appropriate remedy provided under law, cannot, by any strength of reasoning, be termed as 'contemptuous' act or an act aimed at overreaching the process of law.

13 It is not in dispute that alongside the reference proceedings which were pending before the Reference Court (Court of PDJ, Anantnag), the appellant along with other interested persons also Gull Mohammad Bhat Aged 66 Years Son Of ... vs Mr Raj Kumar Goyal Financial ...

4 filed an application under Section 35 of the Act seeking a direction to the Collector to deposit the statutory interest.

Needless to say that under Section 32 of the Act, the Collector, on making of an award under section 11, is under an obligation to tender payment of the compensation awarded by him to the persons interested/entitled thereto.

It is only when the interested persons do not consent to receive it, or there be no person competent to alienate the land, or if there be any dispute as to the title to receive the compensation or as to the apportionment of it, the Collector shall deposit the amount of compensation in the Reference Court.

It is equally true that under Section 35 of the Act, if the amount of compensation awarded is not paid or deposited in the Court, as the case may be,
before taking possession of the land, the Collector shall be liable to pay the awardedamount along with interest at the rate of 6% per annum for a period of one year and at the rate of 10% per annum thereafter till the amount is so paid or deposited.
14

Prima facie, there was nothing wrong with the appellant to file an application under Section 35 to seek a direction to the Collector to deposit the awarded amount along with statutory interest as provided under Section 35 of the Act.
There is also no dispute with regard to the fact that the order dated 27.03.2010 passed by the Court of PDJ, Anantnag was assailed by the respondents unsuccessfully up to the level of Supreme Court.

It is also a fact that while the execution proceedings for compliance of order dated 27.03.2010were pending adjudication before the Court PDJ,
Anantnag, the Reference which was pending before him came to be finally disposed of.
The award/decree passed by the Reference Court disposing of the Reference finally is assailed by the respondents in a regular first appeal pending adjudication before this Court.

It seems that the respondents being of the bonafide opinion that the order dated 27.03.10directing them to deposit the amount awarded by the Collector along with statutory interest had merged with the final order/award passed by the Reference Court, objected to the execution proceedings which were going on before the Court of PDJ, Anantnag even afterfinal disposal of the Reference.

The Executing Court did not entertain the objection and proceeded to pass an order dated 26.03.2022,once again directing the respondents to deposit the accrued statutory interest by or before the next date or else appear in person in the Court

It is this order which was passed by the Court of PDJ, Anantnag in the pending execution proceedings, the respondents was aggrieved of and, accordingly, invoked the supervisory jurisdiction of this Court under Article 227 of the Constitution of India by filing CM(M)
No. 178/2022.The
appellant was arrayed as party respondent and was, thus, well within his right to contest the petition on all available grounds.

It was well available to the appellant to contend before the Court in the proceedings under Article 227 of the Constitution that the petition was not maintainable in view of the finality attained by the order dated 27.03.2010 passed in the execution proceedings which were subjudice before the Court of PDJ, Anantnag after the dismissal/withdrawal of the SLP by the respondents.

He could have raised all these points and contested the claim of the respondents that order dated 27.03.2010 passed by the Court of PDJ,
Anantnag had merged with the final order passed by the same Court.

Instead of contesting the petition filed by the respondents, the appellant devised a novel way of pressuring the respondents to abandon their petition filed under Article 227 of the Constitution of India.

The contempt petition was filed by the appellant alleging that by filing a petition under Article 227 of the Constitution of India, the respondents had overreached the orders passed by the Executing Court which had attained finality after dismissal of SLP filed by the respondents before Supreme Court.

It is true that order impugned in CM(M) No. 178/2022i.e order of PDJ, Anatnag dated 26.03.2022 is in continuation of order dated 27.03.2010 which has admittedly attained finality.
Ordinarily, the order dated 26.03.2022 passed by the PDJ, Anantnag could not have been assailed by the respondents in the face of order dated 27.03.10having attained finality.
However, we cannot brush aside the development that took place after dismissal of the SLP by the Supreme Court.
The Reference Court disposed of the reference proceedings and passed a final award/decree enhancing the compensation awarded by the Collector.

We do not want to say anything on merits, but suffice it to say that the belief and the opinion of the respondentsthat all proceedings before the Court of PDJ,
Anantnag in respect of award had merged with the final order/award passed by the Reference Court was bonafide and the respondents in exercise of their legitimate right of seeking judicial review of the order passed by the Court of PDJ, Anantnag approached this Court by way of a petition under Article 227 of the Constitution of India which is still pending adjudication before this Court.

CM(M)
No.178/2022 which is a petition filed by the respondents under Article 227 of the Constitution is yet to be considered by this Court.
Unless the said petition is taken up for consideration and final orders are passed, it is premature to say that the petition filed by the respondents is an attempt to overreach the process 16

We are in agreement with the view of the learned Single Judge that the petition for initiating contempt proceedingsagainst the respondents was filed by the appellant only to pressurise the respondents not to pursue their petition filed under Article 227 of the Constitution of India and force them to comply with the orders passed by the Court of PDJ, Anantnag.
Such arm-twisting by a litigant by invoking the contempt jurisdiction of this Court unnecessarily cannot be encouraged.
Learned Single Judge was, thus, correct in imposing costs of Rs.25000/- on the appellant for having resorted to such pressurising tactics.
We,therefore, uphold the order of learned Single Judge to the extent it has been challenged before us.
17 For the foregoing reasons, we find no merit in this appeal and the same is, accordingly, dismissed.
(M.A.CHOWDHARY) (SANJEEV KUM  JUDGE JUDGE  Srinagar  12.07.2024  Sanjeev
